title: Graphs in practical situations
summary: A [[travel-graph|travel graph]] shows a journey, and a [[conversion-graph|conversion graph]] changes one unit into another. You'll read and draw both, and find a [[rate-of-change|rate of change]] such as a [[speed|speed]]. Extended adds [[speed-time-graph|speed–time graphs]], [[acceleration|acceleration]] and distance as an area.

goals.text: Read stops, times, distances and speeds from a travel graph.
Use a conversion graph both ways, even past the end of the graph.
Find a rate of change from the [[gradient|gradient]] of a straight line.
Draw a travel graph or a conversion graph from given data.
Find acceleration and deceleration from a speed–time graph, and estimate a gradient by drawing a [[tangent|tangent]].
Find the distance travelled as the area under a speed–time graph.

before.prompt: A runner covers $12$ km in $1$ hour $30$ minutes. Work out her [[average-speed|average speed]] in km/h.
before.hint: Write the time in hours first.
before.explain: $1$ hour $30$ minutes is $1.5$ hours, so the speed is $12 \div 1.5 = 8$ km/h. Revise it in {{lesson:1.12}}.

before.prompt: Write $45$ minutes as a decimal of an hour.
before.hint: There are $60$ minutes in an hour.

blocks.text: A [[travel-graph|travel graph]], or distance–time graph, shows a journey. Time goes across. Distance from the start goes up.
Sloping up: moving away. Sloping down: coming back. Horizontal: stopped. Steeper: faster.

blocks.alt: Travel graph of Leah's bike ride. Time from 08 00 to 12 00 across, with 6 small squares per hour. Distance from home in km up, from 0 to 20, with each small square 2 km. The line rises from home at 08 00 to 8 km at 08 40, is flat at 8 km until 09 00, rises more steeply to 18 km at 09 30, is flat at 18 km until 10 30, then slopes down to home at 12 00.
blocks.caption: Leah's bike ride.

blocks.text: Check the scale first. Here $6$ small squares make an hour, so each is $60 \div 6 = 10$ minutes. Each square up is $2$ km.

blocks.question: Use the travel graph of Leah's bike ride. Work out the total time she spends stopped.
steps: Stops are the horizontal parts.
First stop: at $8$ km from $08\,40$ to $09\,00$, which is $20$ minutes.
Second stop: at $18$ km from $09\,30$ to $10\,30$, which is $60$ minutes.
Total: $20 + 60 = 80$ minutes $= 1$ hour $20$ minutes.

blocks.text: The [[gradient|gradient]] of a straight line measures how steep it is. A line going down from left to right has a negative gradient.

blocks.statement: A [[rate-of-change|rate of change]] is how much one quantity changes per unit of another. On a straight-line graph it is the gradient.
blocks.plain: How fast one thing changes as the other grows.

blocks.text: On a travel graph the gradient is distance $\div$ time, which is the [[speed|speed]].

blocks.question: Use the travel graph of Leah's bike ride. Work out her speed between $09\,00$ and $09\,30$, in km/h.
steps: Change up: $18 - 8 = 10$ km.
Change across: $30$ minutes $= 0.5$ hours.
Speed $=$ gradient $= 10 \div 0.5 = 20$.
Check: half an hour at $20$ km/h is $10$ km.

blocks.prompt: On which part of the ride is Leah travelling fastest?
blocks.hint: Look for the steepest line, not the highest one.

options.text: 09 00 to 09 30, where the line is steepest
09 30 to 10 30, where she is furthest from home

blocks.explain: From $09\,00$ to $09\,30$ she rides at $20$ km/h. The first part is $12$ km/h, and from $09\,30$ to $10\,30$ she is stopped.

verify.truth: 09 00 to 09 30, where the line is steepest

blocks.prompt: Leah rides home from $10\,30$ to $12\,00$ at a constant speed. Work out this speed in km/h.
blocks.hint: She goes from $18$ km back to $0$. Use hours.
blocks.explain: $18 \div 1.5 = 12$ km/h. The gradient is $-12$ because she is coming back, but the speed is $12$ km/h.

sections.heading: Conversion graphs and other real-life graphs

blocks.text: A [[conversion-graph|conversion graph]] changes an amount from one unit or currency into another. Go from the amount you know to the line, then read the other axis.

blocks.alt: Conversion graph between pounds and dollars. Pounds across from 0 to 40, each small square 2 pounds. Dollars up from 0 to 50, each small square 2 dollars. A straight line goes from the origin to 40 pounds and 50 dollars. It passes through 8 pounds and 10 dollars, 16 pounds and 20 dollars, and 24 pounds and 30 dollars.
blocks.caption: Pounds to dollars.

blocks.question: Use the conversion graph to change \$30 into pounds.
steps: Find $30$ on the dollars axis, up the side.
Go across to the line, then down to the pounds axis.
That is $12$ small squares of £2 each, so £24.
Check: £40 is \$50, so £24 is $24 \times \tfrac{50}{40} = 30$ dollars.

blocks.text: A straight line from $(0, 0)$ means direct proportion. So you can scale a reading to go past the end of the graph.

blocks.question: Use the conversion graph to change £200 into dollars.
steps: £200 is past the end of the graph. Scale a reading you can see.
From the graph, £40 is \$50.
$200 = 40 \times 5$, so £200 is $50 \times 5 = 250$ dollars.

blocks.text: The gradient, $50 \div 40 = 1.25$ dollars per pound, is a rate of change: the exchange rate.
A graph that doesn't start at $(0, 0)$, such as a taxi fare with a fixed charge, is not proportion. Don't scale its readings.

blocks.prompt: Use the conversion graph to change £16 into dollars.
blocks.explain: Go up from £16 to the line, then across: \$20. Starting from $16$ on the dollars axis gives about £13, the wrong way round.

blocks.prompt: A taxi fare graph is a straight line from \$4 at $0$ km to \$10 at $5$ km. Work out the charge per km, in dollars.
blocks.explain: $(10 - 4) \div 5 = 1.20$ dollars per km. The \$4 is a fixed charge, so $10$ km costs $4 + 12 = 16$ dollars, not double \$10.

blocks.text: To draw a graph from data, work out the points, label both axes with units, plot small crosses and join them with a ruler.
For a journey, find each part's time from distance $\div$ speed. For a conversion, use $2$ or $3$ values in a [[table-of-values|table of values]].

blocks.question: Sam leaves home at $17\,00$. He walks $6$ km to a friend's house at $4$ km/h. He stays for $50$ minutes, then cycles home at $18$ km/h. Work out the time Sam gets home, then draw his travel graph.
steps: Walk: $6 \div 4 = 1.5$ hours, so he arrives at $18\,30$.
Stay: he leaves at $18\,30 + 50$ minutes $= 19\,20$.
Cycle: $6 \div 18 = \tfrac{1}{3}$ hour $= 20$ minutes, so he is home at $19\,40$.

blocks.alt: Travel graph of Sam's journey. Time from 17 00 to 20 00 across, with 6 small squares per hour. Distance from home in km up, from 0 to 8. Ruled straight lines join home at 17 00, 6 km at 18 30, 6 km at 19 20, and home at 19 40. The four points are marked with dots.
blocks.caption: Cycling home is steeper: it is faster.

blocks.text: Guessing where a line starts. Work out the journey time, then count on or back from a time you know.

blocks.question: Use $1$ gallon $= 4.5$ litres. Draw a conversion graph for $0$ to $10$ gallons. Use it to change $7$ gallons into litres.
steps: Table of values: $0 \to 0$, $4 \to 18$ and $10 \to 45$ litres.
Gallons across, litres up. Label both axes.
Plot the points and draw one ruled line. If they don't line up, recheck a value.
Go up from $7$ gallons to the line, then across: $31.5$ litres.

blocks.prompt: Rosa leaves at $07\,50$ and drives $27$ km at a constant $36$ km/h. At what time does the line on her travel graph end?
blocks.hint: Time $=$ distance $\div$ speed. Then change hours into minutes.
blocks.explain: $27 \div 36 = 0.75$ hours, which is $45$ minutes, not $75$. So $07\,50 + 45$ minutes $= 08\,35$.

blocks.prompt: On your time axis, $5$ small squares make one hour. How many minutes does one small square show?

blocks.text: On a [[speed-time-graph|speed–time graph]], speed goes up. A horizontal line now means constant speed. Stopped means speed $0$.

blocks.alt: Speed-time graph of a tram between two stops. Time in seconds across from 0 to 100, each small square 5 seconds. Speed in metres per second up from 0 to 14, each small square 1 metre per second. The line rises straight from 0 at 0 seconds to 12 at 20 seconds, is flat at 12 until 80 seconds, then falls straight to 0 at 95 seconds.
blocks.caption: A tram between two stops.

blocks.statement: [[acceleration|Acceleration]] is the rate of change of speed. On a speed–time graph it is the gradient.
blocks.plain: How quickly the speed is changing.

blocks.text: Its unit is m/s per second, written m/s$^2$. A downward slope is a deceleration, given as a positive number.

blocks.question: Use the tram's speed–time graph. Work out its acceleration in the first $20$ seconds.
steps: In the first $20$ s the speed goes from $0$ to $12$ m/s.
Acceleration $=$ gradient $= \frac{12 - 0}{20} = 0.6$.

blocks.prompt: Use the tram's graph. Work out its deceleration between $80$ and $95$ seconds.
blocks.hint: How long does the speed take to drop from $12$ m/s to $0$?
blocks.explain: The speed falls by $12$ m/s in $95 - 80 = 15$ s: $12 \div 15 = 0.8$ m/s$^2$.

blocks.text: On a curve the gradient keeps changing. To estimate it at a point, draw the [[tangent|tangent]] there and find its gradient.

blocks.alt: Distance-time graph of a ball rolling down a slope. Time in seconds across from 0 to 6, each small square half a second. Distance in metres up from 0 to 18, each small square 1 metre. The curve starts flat at the origin and gets steeper, reaching 18 metres at 6 seconds. A dashed tangent touches the curve at 4 seconds, 8 metres. The tangent passes through 2 seconds, 0 metres and 6 seconds, 16 metres, both marked with dots.
blocks.caption: The dashed tangent touches the curve at $4$ seconds.

blocks.question: The graph shows the distance travelled by a ball rolling down a slope. By drawing a tangent, estimate the speed of the ball at $4$ seconds.
steps: Place a ruler so it touches the curve at $4$ seconds without cutting across it. Draw the tangent.
Read two points far apart on it: $(2, 0)$ and $(6, 16)$.
Gradient $= \frac{16 - 0}{6 - 2} = 4$.
The gradient of a distance–time graph is the speed. A slightly different tangent gives a slightly different estimate.

blocks.text: Joining the origin to the curve. That gives the average speed so far, not the speed at that moment.

blocks.prompt: You want the speed of the ball at exactly $3$ seconds. Which line do you find the gradient of?
blocks.hint: It must match the curve's steepness at that one point.

options.text: The line from the origin to the curve at 3 seconds
The line joining the curve at 0 and 6 seconds

blocks.explain: Only the tangent has the curve's steepness at $3$ seconds. The other lines give average speeds over a time interval.

sections.heading: Distance from the area under a speed–time graph

blocks.text: At a constant speed, distance $=$ speed $\times$ time: the area of a rectangle under the graph. For any speed–time graph, the area under it is the distance travelled.
Split the area at each corner into rectangles, triangles and trapezia. The triangle area formula is on the formula list.
Here $a$ and $b$ are the parallel sides and $h$ is the gap between them.

blocks.question: Use the tram's speed–time graph. Work out the distance the tram travels between the two stops.
steps: Split the area at $20$ s and $80$ s.
Triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 12 = 120$ m.
Rectangle: $60 \times 12 = 720$ m.
Triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 12 = 90$ m.
Total: $120 + 720 + 90 = 930$ m. Check: one trapezium, $\tfrac{1}{2}(60 + 95) \times 12 = 930$.

blocks.text: Treating the whole graph as one triangle, or missing a piece. Split at every corner.

blocks.prompt: Work out the tram's average speed over the whole $95$ seconds. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Average speed $=$ total distance $\div$ total time.
blocks.explain: $930 \div 95 = 9.789\ldots$, so $9.79$ m/s. Dividing by $80$ or $60$ leaves out time.

blocks.question: An e-scooter starts from rest and speeds up steadily to $6$ m/s in $8$ seconds. It then travels at $6$ m/s until time $T$ seconds. By then it has travelled $156$ m. Work out $T$.
steps: Sketch it: a slope from $(0, 0)$ to $(8, 6)$, then flat to $(T, 6)$.
Triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 6 = 24$ m.
Rectangle: $156 - 24 = 132$ m, so its width is $132 \div 6 = 22$ s.

blocks.text: Giving $22$, the rectangle's width, as $T$. Add the first $8$ seconds.

blocks.prompt: A jogger speeds up steadily from rest to $4$ m/s in $6$ s. She runs at $4$ m/s for $50$ s, then slows steadily to rest in $4$ s. Work out the total distance she runs, in metres.

blocks.text: Travel graph: horizontal means stopped, steeper means faster, and the gradient is the speed (ignore the minus sign on the way back).
Gradient $=$ change up $\div$ change across: a rate of change, such as km/h.
Conversion graph through $(0, 0)$: you can scale a reading. Not through $(0, 0)$: you can't.
Speed–time graph: horizontal means constant speed, and the gradient is the acceleration.
Distance $=$ area under a speed–time graph.
Gradient at a point on a curve: draw the tangent, then use two points far apart on it.

mistakes: Taking each small square as $5$ minutes. Count the squares in one hour first: $6$ squares means $10$ minutes each.
Saying a horizontal line on a travel graph means steady speed. It means stopped.
Writing $2.15$ hours as $2$ hours $15$ minutes. $0.15 \times 60 = 9$, so it is $2$ hours $9$ minutes.
Leaving a speed in km per minute, or leaving out a stop. Use hours, and include stops in the total time.
examTips: Write down a reading from a graph: no working is needed, but check what one small square is worth.
Complete the travel graph: write the journey-time calculation, then rule a straight line. The calculation can earn a mark on its own.
Explain what is happening: describe the line in words, such as "stopped, because the line is horizontal".
Extended: by drawing a tangent, find an estimate: draw it, then show the two points you used and the division.
